course.title: Machine Learning for Tabular Data: Baselines and Validation

questions.prompt: The advisers can agree 800 support plans a year, starting in week 3 of a programme. Which framing fits?
options: One row per trainee: will this trainee ever leave a programme?
One row per enrolment, at exit: did the trainee complete?
One row per provider and year: how many trainees will leave?
One row per enrolment, at the end of week 2: will the trainee not complete?
questions.explanation: The unit and the moment come from the action: one support plan per enrolment, agreed in week 3.
misconceptions: Takes the trainee as the unit: one trainee has several enrolments with different risks, and the adviser acts on one of them
Puts the moment at exit: by then the place is lost and no support plan can change it
Predicts a total for planning, which is a different decision: the advisers need names, not a count

questions.prompt: Loay reports that his model reaches an average precision of 0.30 on a split of his own. What is the right reply?
options: It is poor: the model is wrong 70% of the time
It cannot be judged until it stands beside the constant and the rules on the same folds
It is good: it is well above the base rate of 0.12
It is slightly worse than the rules, which score 0.31
questions.explanation: A score is read against the rungs below it, and only on the same rows.
misconceptions: Reads average precision like accuracy: 0.30 is not 30% correct, and its floor here is 0.12, not 0.5
Compares with the floor only: it beats a constant, but three rules on a card score 0.31 on the fund's folds
Treats a score as comparable across splits: a different split has different rows and a different base rate

questions.prompt: You score a logistic model on five folds. On which rows is the scaler of fold 3 fitted?
options: On the training rows of fold 3 only, each time the pipeline is fitted
On all development rows, once, before the folds are made
On the validation rows of fold 3, so that they are scaled correctly
On the 2025 cohort, because it is the most recent
questions.explanation: Preparation is part of the model, and a model learns from training rows only.
misconceptions: Fits once before splitting: the validation rows of every fold have then shaped their own preparation
Fits on the rows being scored: at prediction time the model would need a batch of future rows to prepare one
Uses the closed cohort: the holdout must stay untouched until the final check on Day 4

questions.prompt: Four candidate features for a row scored at the end of week 2. Which one fails the time-travel test?
options: The number of the trainee's enrolments that ended before the prediction date
The trainee's entry test score
The trainee's non-completion rate over all of their enrolments in the table
The trainee's days absent in the first two weeks of this programme
questions.explanation: "All enrolments in the table" includes later ones and the row itself: their outcomes did not exist on the prediction date.
misconceptions: Suspects a strong, legitimate feature: an enrolment that ended before the prediction date had a known outcome that day
Mistakes a registration fact for an outcome: the entry test is taken before the first enrolment
Confuses a week-2 fact with a later one: the register of the first two weeks exists on the prediction date

questions.prompt: Two history features lifted the logistic rung from 0.501 to 0.524. The fold spread of that rung is 0.028. Why is the gain still believable?
options: Because 0.023 is large compared with the base rate of 0.12
Because the table has 32,000 development rows
Because the gain has the same sign on all five folds, where both models met the same rows
Because the features passed the time-travel test
questions.explanation: A difference is judged fold by fold. Five gains of +0.012 to +0.031 on the same rows say more than two means and a spread.
misconceptions: Compares the gain with the base rate, which says nothing about whether the gain is noise
Trusts the size of the table: many rows shrink noise but do not show that this difference is outside it
Takes passing the time-travel test as proof of usefulness: the test shows the features read the past only

questions.prompt: A boosted model scores 0.85 on its 9,068 training rows and 0.50 on the validation rows of the same fold. What do you conclude?
options: The model has memorised part of the training rows; 0.50 is the number to log
The true score is about halfway, near 0.67
The validation rows must contain a leak
The validation fold is unusually hard and should be replaced
questions.explanation: A training score measures how flexible the model is. Only rows the model has not seen estimate how it will do.
misconceptions: Averages memory and generalisation: the training score is not an estimate of anything the advisers will see
Reads a large gap as a leak: leakage inflates the validation score, and here it is the training score that is high
Blames the validation fold: its rows are simply the ones the model has not seen, which is their purpose

questions.prompt: An analyst tries 200 settings, scores each on the same five folds and reports the highest mean, 0.547. What is wrong with the number?
options: 200 trials are too many for a table of this size
Random search is unreliable; a grid would give the true score
Five folds are too few to score any model
The folds that chose the winner also score it, so part of 0.547 is luck
questions.explanation: The best of 200 on a set of rows is biased upward on those rows. Choose on inner folds; report on rows no trial has seen.
misconceptions: Blames the amount of search: more trials are fine when the choice and the report use different rows
Blames the method of search: a grid would have the same fault, because the fault is where the winner is scored
Expects the folds themselves to be at fault: they are fine for scoring one model fixed in advance

questions.prompt: A team reports that an automated tool beats their tuned model, 0.561 to 0.529. Which detail makes the comparison worthless?
options: The tool blends several models and the champion is one model
The tool's 0.561 is its own internal validation score; the champion's 0.529 is on the fund's folds
The tool was told to optimise average precision
Both ran with a limit of 28 seconds a fold
questions.explanation: Two scores compare only on the same rows. The tool's own number sits on a random split it made inside the training rows.
misconceptions: Objects to a difference in kind: a challenger is allowed to be a blend, that is the point of testing it
Objects to the metric being shared: both sides should be optimised for the metric that is reported
Objects to equal budgets: the same time limit is what makes the contest fair

questions.prompt: A challenger's mean paired difference is +0.006, with a 95% interval from −0.004 to +0.016. The minimum effect stated in advance is +0.01. What is the decision?
options: Adopt the challenger: its mean difference is positive
The two models are shown to be equal
Not shown: the interval straddles the minimum effect, so the champion stays
Adopt it, with the minimum effect lowered to +0.005
questions.explanation: The interval holds values on both sides of +0.01. The rule fixed in advance says the simpler model stays until more folds or more rows settle it.
misconceptions: Reads the mean alone: +0.006 is positive, but the interval reaches below zero and below the minimum effect
Reads an interval containing zero as proof of equality: the data are also compatible with a gain of +0.016
Lowers the bar after seeing the result: a minimum effect moved to fit the data is no longer a rule

questions.prompt: The challenger differed from the champion by −0.007 (95% interval −0.018 to +0.004). The minimum effect was +0.01. Why was the decision "keep the champion" and not "not shown"?
options: Because the mean difference is negative
Because the whole interval lies below the minimum effect
Because the interval excludes zero
Because the champion won on three of the five folds
questions.explanation: The upper end, +0.004, is below +0.01: even the most favourable value the data allow is not worth a blend of seven models.
misconceptions: Reads the sign of the mean alone: a negative mean with an interval reaching above the minimum effect would be 'not shown'
Requires the interval to exclude zero: the rule compares the interval with the minimum effect, not with zero
Counts folds: three of five is not a rule that was stated, and it ignores the size of the differences

questions.prompt: The fund wants to offer Mubakkir to a partner fund in another country. None of its trainees has ever enrolled with Sullam. Which score from Lab 3.1 comes closest to what the partner should expect?
options: The time-ordered score, 0.525
The random score, 0.521
The grouped score with history hidden, 0.500, and even that with caution
The score of returning trainees, 0.578
questions.explanation: In that use every trainee is new. The grouped split with hidden history rehearses it; other providers and another country are further differences no split of this table can rehearse.
misconceptions: Picks the highest honest score: it includes returning trainees with a history, which the partner does not have
Assumes rows like these from the same period: the partner's trainees are all new, with no history
Takes the score of returning trainees for everyone: it is the best case, earned with history columns

questions.prompt: A bank predicts which customers will close their account next month. One feature is the number of calls the customer made to the retention desk. Customers are transferred to that desk when they ask to close the account. Which kind of leak is this?
options: Target leakage
Preparation leakage
Group contamination
No leak: call behaviour is a legitimate feature
questions.explanation: The column is a consequence of the outcome: a call to that desk is made after the customer has decided. Calls to the general helpline would be a fair feature.
misconceptions: Looks for a step fitted before the split: nothing was fitted here, the column itself carries the outcome
Looks for repeated customers across the split: the fault would remain with every customer on one side
Treats call counts as ordinary behaviour: these calls exist only because the customer has asked to leave

questions.prompt: A received table scores far above your ladder. Its data dictionary lists when every recorded column is written. Twelve further columns were computed by a colleague. Where do you start?
options: Tune the model again on the received table
Drop all twelve computed columns
Switch to a time-ordered split and compare
Read the dictionary for columns recorded after the prediction time, then rank the rest by importance
questions.explanation: The cheapest instrument goes first. The dictionary costs nothing; importance then tells you which of the twelve computed columns to rebuild first.
misconceptions: Starts with the most expensive step: a new search cannot repair a column that knows the answer
Removes everything computed: an audit also clears honest columns, and history is the fund's best information
Changes the split before the columns: a target leak scores just as well under any split

questions.prompt: A vendor's slide says: "Our model predicts non-completion with 91% accuracy." Which question tells you most, fastest?
options: Which algorithm does the model use?
How many rows was it trained on?
What share of the test rows completed, and what does "everyone completes" score on them?
What is its area under the curve?
questions.explanation: If 88% of the test rows completed, 91% accuracy is three points above an answer that needs no model. The baseline on the same rows turns a number into information.
misconceptions: Asks about the model family: the algorithm does not tell you whether the number means anything
Asks about the amount of training data: more rows do not repair a metric that a constant answer can reach
Asks for a different summary of the same unknown test: without the rows and the baseline it is as hard to read

questions.prompt: In the received table, trainee_noncompletions equalled the past-only count on 84% of the rows and carried 80% of the model's gain. Which kind of leak is it?
options: Group or duplicate contamination
Preparation leakage
No leak: a history of non-completion is a fair feature
Future information
questions.explanation: The idea of the feature is fair; its construction counted this enrolment and later ones. On the prediction day those outcomes did not exist.
misconceptions: Looks for a repeated row or person across the split: the column would leak under any split, with every trainee on one side
Looks for a step fitted before the split: nothing was fitted, the column was counted from the wrong records
Trusts the 84% of rows where it agrees with the honest count: the other 16% hold the outcome being predicted

questions.prompt: The fund keeps the threshold of 0.41. Next year a new programme doubles the intake, with trainees much like this year's. What happens?
options: The list roughly doubles to 1,600 names, twice what the advisers can support
The list stays at 800, because the threshold was chosen for 800
Precision halves, because there are twice as many trainees
The scores fall, so fewer trainees pass the threshold
questions.explanation: A threshold lists everyone above a risk level. Twice the trainees at the same risk levels means twice the names. Only a rule on the list length follows capacity.
misconceptions: Assumes the threshold adapts to capacity: a threshold is a fixed number and knows nothing about plans
Confuses the size of the cohort with the quality of the ranking: similar trainees give similar precision
Assumes more rows change the scores of individual trainees: each score depends on the trainee's own columns

questions.prompt: Two models have the same average precision. Model A's scores average 0.14, model B's 0.40; 13.5% of the cohort left. The fund wants to list everyone above the break-even probability, 0.20. Which statement holds?
options: Either model can be used: they rank equally well
Only model A's scores can be compared with 0.20, after checking them by decile
Model B is better: it is more confident about the trainees at risk
Use the mean of the two scores
questions.explanation: A break-even probability is a statement about real rates. Only a calibrated score can be compared with it.
misconceptions: Takes equal ranking for equal meaning: above 0.20, model B lists most of the cohort
Prefers higher scores as if they were stronger signals: B's scores are high because of how it was trained
Averages two scales that mean different things: the result is calibrated on neither

questions.prompt: In one region 12 trainees left and 9 of them were not on the list: a miss rate of 0.75, interval 0.47 to 0.91. The cohort's rate is 0.62. What do you report?
options: The model fails this region: 0.75 is far above 0.62
The region is fine: its interval contains 0.62
Leave the region out of the table: the slice is too small
The rate with its interval, and that 12 cases cannot tell; pool with later cohorts
questions.explanation: The interval is the finding: with 12 cases the data are compatible with a rate below the cohort's and with one far above it. Saying so, and how to learn more, is the honest report.
misconceptions: Reads the rate without its interval: nine of twelve is compatible with the cohort's rate
Reads an interval that contains 0.62 as proof of no difference: it also contains 0.90
Removes the evidence that the slice is small: a table without it would hide that nothing is known

questions.prompt: You may add one sentence to the limits of Mubakkir's card. Which one helps its readers most?
options: "The model uses gradient-boosted trees with 400 trees of 8 leaves."
"Results may vary on new data."
"Not validated for trainees in their first two weeks: they have no early-absence record."
"The model achieves an average precision of 0.55 on held-out data."
questions.explanation: A limit names a situation the validation never covered, in words a reader can recognise. Mubakkir scores trainees still enrolled at the end of week 2 and was never tested on anyone else.
misconceptions: States a method, not a limit: it tells the reader nothing about when the scores fail
Is true of every model: the reader cannot recognise a situation or act on it
Repeats a result as if it were a guarantee: the card should say where it does not hold

questions.prompt: A hospital wants to phone patients who are likely to miss a follow-up visit. The phone team works two days before each visit. When is the prediction made?
options: When the patient is first registered
On the morning of the visit
Two days before the visit
After the visit, when attendance is recorded
questions.explanation: The prediction time is the moment the action is taken: the calls are made two days before the visit, so everything the model reads must exist by then.
misconceptions: Chooses the earliest moment: most of what predicts a missed visit (the booking, earlier visits) does not exist at registration
Chooses a moment after the action: the phone team has already finished its calls
Takes the moment the outcome is recorded: nothing is left to decide then

questions.prompt: Of 45,000 enrolments, 16.7% are not completed. A model scores trainees at the end of week 2; 2,444 trainees have left by then. Which base rate does the model have to beat?
options: 16.7%, the rate of all enrolments
The rate among the trainees still enrolled at the end of week 2
The rate among the 2,444 who left early
50%, because there are two classes
questions.explanation: The model is judged on the rows it can score. The trainees who have already left are outside its population, and the rate of the rest is lower (11.9%).
misconceptions: Uses the whole export: a third of the non-completers are gone before the model can score them
Looks at the rows the model never sees: all of them are non-completers by definition
Confuses the number of classes with their frequencies

questions.prompt: A support plan costs SAR 450. A lost place costs SAR 9,000. One supported non-completer in four then completes. Above which probability of not completing does a plan pay for itself?
questions.explanation: A plan pays when p x 0.25 x 9,000 is more than 450, so when p is above 0.20.
misconceptions: Divides the cost of the plan by the cost of the place and forgets that support works only one time in four
Takes the success rate of support as the threshold
Falls back on the default threshold of a classifier, which ignores the costs

questions.prompt: In a validation fold 11% of trainees do not complete. A predictor gives every trainee the same score. What is its average precision?
questions.explanation: With no information the precision is the base rate at every position of the ranking, so the average precision is the base rate.
misconceptions: Assumes that a useless ranking finds nobody: at any depth it still finds the base rate
Reports the accuracy of predicting the majority class
Uses the floor of ROC AUC, which is 0.5 whatever the base rate

questions.prompt: Model A scores 0.52 on five time-ordered folds. A colleague scores model B at 0.55 on five random folds of the same table. What can you say?
options: B is better by 0.03
A is better, because time-ordered folds are harder
Nothing yet: the two models were scored on different rows
They are equal within the fold spread
questions.explanation: Scores compare only on the same folds: different rows have different base rates and different difficulty.
misconceptions: Subtracts two numbers that were measured on different rows
Guesses the size of the difference between the schemes; it has to be measured
Uses a spread that neither run has shown

questions.prompt: An analyst fills missing ages with the median of the whole table, then cross-validates a model. What kind of fault is this?
options: Target leakage: the median is computed from the outcome
Preparation leakage: a statistic was fitted on rows that are later held out
Group contamination: the same person is on both sides
No fault: a median does not use the outcome
questions.explanation: The median has read the held-out rows. The harm is usually small for a statistic that ignores the outcome, but the step belongs inside the pipeline, fitted on training rows only.
misconceptions: Mistakes the kind: the median of age does not involve the outcome
Names a fault of the split, which is not described here
Treats "does not use the outcome" as "has not seen the held-out rows": the rule is about the rows

questions.prompt: A library network groups its 900 members with k-means (k = 3) on two columns: loans a year (5 to 819) and the share of loans that are e-books (0 to 0.93). The three segments have mean loans of 45, 132 and 322, and mean e-book shares of 0.38, 0.37 and 0.33. What do you conclude?
options: Members hardly differ in how much they read e-books
Only loans shaped the segments: scale both columns and run again
Three segments are too few: raise k until the e-book share differs
The segments are sound: k-means made each one as tight as it could
questions.explanation: Loans run into the hundreds and the share stays between 0 and 1, so the Euclidean distance is almost all loans: the segments differ in loans and not in e-book use. Scaled, the same members split into print readers (e-book share 0.15), heavy e-book readers (0.70) and a small group of very frequent borrowers.
misconceptions: Reads the segment means as the data: the share itself runs from 0 to 0.93, the segments simply ignored it
Treats a problem of units as a problem of k: more segments still cut along loans first
Takes the tightest segments for the right ones: they are tightest for a distance that is nearly all loans

questions.prompt: A row is scored on 20 April. The same trainee has an earlier enrolment that started in January and ended in September of the same year. May its outcome be used as a history feature for the April row?
options: Yes, it started earlier
Yes, if the model is validated on time-ordered folds
No, its outcome was not known on 20 April
Only if the trainee completed it
questions.explanation: A history feature may read records whose outcome was known at the prediction time. This one ended five months later.
misconceptions: Reads "earlier" as "started earlier": the outcome is what matters, and it came in September
Expects the split to repair a feature: no split removes information that is inside a column
Makes the rule depend on the outcome itself, which is exactly what is unknown

questions.prompt: A boosted model scores 0.90 on its training rows and 0.48 on the validation rows of the same fold. A logistic model scores 0.52 and 0.50. Which model goes further up the ladder?
options: The boosted model: its training score shows what it can reach
The boosted model, after averaging its two scores
Neither: the gap of the boosted model proves a leak
The logistic model: only validation scores are compared
questions.explanation: A rung is its score on rows the model has not seen. On those the logistic model is ahead, 0.50 to 0.48.
misconceptions: Reads a training score as potential: it measures how much the model memorised
Averages memory and generalisation into a number that estimates neither
Takes a large train-validation gap for leakage: a leak inflates the validation score, not the training score

questions.prompt: A team wants to tune a boosted model on a table of 30,000 rows. Which plan keeps the reported score honest?
options: Try settings until the validation score stops improving, then report it
Tune on the test set, since it is the most recent data
Run a full grid of 2,000 settings and report the best mean over the folds
Fix 20 random trials in advance, choose on inner folds, report on the outer folds
questions.explanation: A stated budget fixes how often the validation rows are looked at, and nested folds keep the rows that choose apart from the rows that report.
misconceptions: Stops when the score looks good: the number of looks is undefined, so the best score cannot be interpreted
Spends the test set on choosing: nothing is left to report on
Reports the best of 2,000 on the folds that chose it: part of that score is luck

questions.prompt: A nested search picks different settings in each of five outer folds and reports a mean of 0.53. What does 0.53 describe?
options: The settings that were chosen most often
Nothing usable, because the settings disagree
The best of the five sets of settings
The procedure: search under this budget, then fit
questions.explanation: Nested validation scores the whole procedure. The model that is used comes from running that procedure once on all development rows.
misconceptions: Looks for one winner among the folds: the nested score is not the score of any single set of settings
Expects the folds to agree: different training parts may reasonably choose different settings
Reads a mean as a maximum

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes a pretrained tabular model, called through its vendor's hosted service, as a challenger for a model on patient records. What do you settle before any score is computed?
options: Whether its published benchmark results are better than yours
Whether it runs faster than your tuned model
Whether it supports the same number of features
Whether the licence allows this use and whether the records may leave your machines
questions.explanation: A challenger that may not be used, or that needs data to go where they may not go, has lost before the contest starts, whatever it scores.
misconceptions: Trusts a benchmark on other tables: it says nothing about permission to use the model or about your data
Compares speed before legality and data protection
Checks a technical detail first: it matters only if the model may be used at all

questions.prompt: An automated tool is given two hours and reports 0.58 from its own internal validation. Your tuned model took three minutes and scores 0.53 on your five time-ordered folds. What does the comparison show?
options: The tool is better by 0.05
Your model is better, because it is faster
Nothing: different rows, different budgets
The tool overfits, because its score is higher
questions.explanation: A contest fixes the folds and the budget for both sides. The tool's own number sits on a split it chose, and it had forty times the time.
misconceptions: Subtracts scores measured on different rows under different budgets
Declares a winner on speed alone, without a score on common rows
Infers overfitting from a higher number: it may or may not be true, and only your folds can tell

questions.prompt: Two models are scored on the same five folds. Model A: mean 0.530, fold spread 0.020. Model B: mean 0.540, fold spread 0.021. B is ahead on all five folds, by 0.008 to 0.012. What do you conclude?
options: B is ahead: the five paired differences are all positive and close together
No difference: 0.010 is inside both spreads
A is better: its spread is smaller
Nothing can be said with five folds
questions.explanation: The folds pair the models. Most of each spread is the difficulty of the fold, shared by both; the differences vary far less than the scores.
misconceptions: Compares two means with their spreads and throws the pairing away
Chooses on the spread and ignores the paired differences
Gives up on few folds: five consistent differences are informative, and an interval says how much

questions.prompt: A challenger's mean paired difference is +0.021 with a 95% interval from +0.013 to +0.029. The minimum effect stated in advance is +0.01. What is the decision?
options: Not shown: keep the champion
Keep the champion
Adopt the challenger
Lower the minimum effect and test again
questions.explanation: The whole interval lies above the minimum effect, so the gain is both shown and large enough to matter.
misconceptions: Calls it not shown although the interval does not contain the minimum effect
Ignores an interval that lies entirely above the bar set in advance
Changes a rule after seeing the result, when the result already meets the rule

questions.prompt: Why is the minimum effect for adopting a challenger written down before the contest is run?
options: So that the bar cannot drift to just below whatever was measured
So that the interval becomes narrower
Because the t distribution requires it
So that fewer folds are needed
questions.explanation: A rule chosen after the result is not a rule. The minimum effect is a judgment about cost and benefit, made without knowing who won.
misconceptions: Expects a written threshold to change the statistics: the interval depends on the data only
Looks for a mathematical requirement where the reason is honesty of the procedure
Confuses the decision rule with the amount of evidence

questions.prompt: A model predicts equipment failure from daily readings of 50 machines, a year of rows per machine. It will be installed on 30 machines that are delivered next month. Which validation split rehearses that use?
options: A grouped split: all rows of a machine on one side
A random split of the daily rows
A time-ordered split of all machines together
A random split, stratified by failure
questions.explanation: In use every machine is new to the model. Validation rows therefore have to come from machines that are in no training row.
misconceptions: Lets the model meet each machine in training and in validation: it is scored on machines it knows
Orders time and keeps every machine on both sides: the unit that is new in use is the machine
Balances the outcome across folds and leaves the shared machines in place

questions.prompt: Loans are repaid over twelve months, and default is recorded when it happens. On 1 July a team trains on "all loans with a known outcome". Which loans from the last twelve months are in the training rows?
options: All of them
None of them
Only those that have already defaulted
A random sample of them
questions.explanation: A recent loan has a known outcome only if it has already defaulted; the good ones are still running. The model then learns that recent loans always fail. Training rows should be loans whose twelve months had passed.
misconceptions: Assumes every recent loan has an outcome: the ones still being repaid have none yet
Assumes no recent loan has an outcome: the early defaults do
Treats the selection as random: it depends on the outcome itself

questions.prompt: On one table a model scores 0.52 under a random split and 0.53 under time-ordered folds, with fold spreads of 0.02. What do you write in the validation section?
options: The random split overstates performance, as it always does
The time-ordered folds are faulty: they should score lower
Both were measured; no gap is shown for this model; the time-ordered folds are kept because they rehearse the use
The splits are interchangeable from now on
questions.explanation: A gap between splits is measured, and here none is shown. The scheme is still chosen from the use, and the result holds only for this model and these features.
misconceptions: Repeats a rule of thumb against the measurement
Expects a direction and doubts the folds when it does not appear
Generalises one measurement to every later model and feature

questions.prompt: Why can a random split not show how much a model loses when it is used a year after training?
options: Because it trains and validates on rows from the same period
Because random folds are smaller
Because it does not stratify by year
Because it uses fewer trees
questions.explanation: Under a random split the training rows are as recent as the validation rows, so the model is always fresh. Only a split ordered in time can score an old model on later rows.
misconceptions: Looks at the size of the folds: the issue is which period the rows come from
Asks for the same mix of years on both sides, which is the opposite of what an ageing test needs
Confuses a setting of the model with the design of the split

questions.prompt: A churn model uses each customer's past complaints as features. Time-ordered folds give 0.55. The company wants to use it in a new country where no customer has any past. Which estimate is the most relevant?
options: 0.55, the time-ordered score
The score with history features hidden for the validation rows
The score of the customers with the longest history
The training score
questions.explanation: In the new use nobody has a history. Hiding it for validation customers rehearses that; even then another country differs in ways no split of this table can show.
misconceptions: Quotes a score that was partly earned with features the new customers will not have
Picks the best-served group as if it stood for everyone
Reports how well the model fits rows it has seen

questions.prompt: A model predicts which insurance claims are fraudulent when they are filed. One feature is "assigned to the special investigations unit". Claims are sent to that unit when a handler suspects fraud. What is this?
options: A legitimate feature
Preparation leakage
Group contamination
Target leakage
questions.explanation: The column records a person's answer to the question the model is asked, and it is written after filing. It will not exist when a new claim is scored.
misconceptions: Accepts a column because it is strongly related to the outcome, which is exactly the warning sign
Looks for a step fitted before the split: the fault is in the column itself
Looks for the same claim on both sides: the column leaks under any split

questions.prompt: A model scores each order for the risk of a return on the day it ships. One feature is the customer's return rate, computed over all of the customer's orders in the table. What is the fault?
options: Preparation leakage: the rate should be scaled inside the pipeline
None: the rate describes the customer
Group contamination: customers repeat
Future information: the rate includes later orders and this one
questions.explanation: On the shipping day only earlier orders have an outcome. The rate has to be rebuilt for each row from orders whose outcome was known by then.
misconceptions: Sees a preparation problem in a feature that reads the future
Accepts the feature for its meaning without asking from which rows it was computed
Names the repeated customers: grouping them would not remove what the column has read

questions.prompt: A table has one row per student, measured in one term. A model will be used on next term's students of the same schools; teaching and grading rules change little. Before cross-validation, the analyst kept the 15 of 400 columns most correlated with the outcome, using all rows. Which pair is right?
options: Target leakage; a time-ordered split
Preparation leakage; a random split with the selection inside each fold
No leak; a random split
Group contamination; a grouped split by student
questions.explanation: The selection is a step fitted on rows that later score the model. The split itself is sound here: each student is one independent row.
misconceptions: Calls a selection step a target leak and asks for time order where there is one term
Overlooks a step that used the outcome of the held-out rows
Looks for repeated students where each has one row

questions.prompt: A received table has unique record keys. You suspect that some records were entered twice when two systems were merged. How do you check?
options: Count duplicated keys
Look for rows that agree on the columns describing the real event
Sort by importance and inspect the top feature
Switch to a time-ordered split
questions.explanation: A copy made under a new key passes any test of the key. The test is on what identifies the event: who, where, when.
misconceptions: Tests the key, which the merge made unique
Uses the instrument for column leaks on a problem of rows
Changes the split: copies with the same date stay together and still count twice

questions.prompt: During an audit a team removes five suspicious columns at once, and the score falls from 0.95 to 0.55. What is lost by doing it this way?
options: Which columns were leaks, how much each mattered, and whether an honest one was thrown out
Nothing: the final score is what matters
The reproducibility of the run
The calibration of the model
questions.explanation: One removal at a time, with the score before and after, tells you what each column carried and lets an audit clear the honest ones.
misconceptions: Settles for the end result and learns nothing for the next table
Confuses the audit trail with the seed
Names an unrelated property of the model

questions.prompt: A notebook reports 94% accuracy for predicting a fault that occurs in 5% of units. What do you ask first?
options: What a constant answer scores on the same test rows, and what share of them had the fault
Which library was used
Whether the learning rate was tuned
How long training took
questions.explanation: If 5% of the test rows have the fault, "no fault" is 95% accurate. A baseline on the same rows turns the number into information.
misconceptions: Asks about tools before asking whether the number means anything
Asks about tuning a model whose score may be below a constant answer
Asks about cost before value

questions.prompt: A team of nurses can make 300 follow-up calls a month. A model scores 4,000 patients a month for the risk of readmission, which happens to 8% of them. Where does the threshold come from?
options: 0.5, the default of the library
0.08, the base rate
The score of the 300th highest-ranked patient
The score that maximises accuracy
questions.explanation: Capacity decides the length of the list, and the list decides the cut. The precision and recall of that list are then reported.
misconceptions: Uses a default that nothing in the decision produces
Takes the base rate for a threshold: about half the patients may lie above it
Optimises a metric that rewards calling nobody when the outcome is rare

questions.prompt: A list of 500 names has precision 0.60 and recall 0.35. Which sentence is right?
options: 60% of the people at risk are on the list
The model is right 60% of the time
35% of the list had the outcome
Of the people who went on to have the outcome, about a third were on the list
questions.explanation: Recall is counted among those who had the outcome; precision among those on the list. Here 300 of 500 on the list had the outcome, and they are 35% of all who did.
misconceptions: Reads precision as if it were recall
Reads precision as accuracy over everyone
Reads recall as if it were precision

questions.prompt: A model trained with class weights ranks as well as an unweighted one. Its scores average 0.38 where 12% have the outcome. For which use is it unfit as it is?
options: Listing the 500 highest-ranked people
Comparing average precision between the two models
Listing everyone whose probability exceeds a break-even of 0.25
Sorting people for a first review
questions.explanation: A break-even probability is a statement about real rates. Scores that average three times the observed rate cannot be compared with it until they are calibrated.
misconceptions: Picks a use that needs only the order, which is intact
Picks a metric that depends only on the order
Picks another use of the order alone

questions.prompt: On which rows should a calibrator be fitted?
options: The training rows of the model, which are the most numerous
The final test rows, which are the most recent
Rows the model was not trained on, kept apart from the final test rows
Any rows, since a calibrator has only two parameters
questions.explanation: On its own training rows a model's scores fit too well, and a calibrator fitted there learns to trust them too much. The final test rows must stay unseen by every fitted step.
misconceptions: Fits on rows the model has partly memorised
Spends the test rows on fitting, so nothing honest is left to report
Assumes a small model cannot overfit to the wrong rows

questions.prompt: Among people who had the outcome, the model missed 9 of 12 in district A (75%) and 300 of 500 in district B (60%). The overall miss rate is 61%. What can you say about district A?
options: The model is unfair to district A
District A should be dropped from the report
District A is fine, because its interval contains 61%
With 12 cases the interval is wide and contains 61%: too few to tell
questions.explanation: The 95% interval for 9 of 12 runs from about 47% to 91%. It is compatible with the overall rate and with far worse; the honest report gives the interval and says more cases are needed.
misconceptions: Reads a rate without its interval
Removes the evidence that the slice is small, and with it the reason to keep looking
Takes an interval that contains the overall rate as proof of no difference

questions.prompt: A model that predicts missed medical appointments uses the number of earlier reminders sent to each patient. In rural clinics reminders are made by phone and are often not logged. Rural patients who miss appointments are flagged less often. Which bias type of the SDAIA AI Bias Reference Guide fits?
options: Measurement bias
Coverage bias
Sample size bias
Aggregation bias
questions.explanation: The feature is recorded differently for one group, so it means something different there. The remedy is in the recording, not in the algorithm.
misconceptions: Names under-representation: the rural patients are in the data, their feature is mis-recorded
Names small numbers: the finding is about how a column is recorded
Names a hidden average: that describes the reporting, not the cause

questions.prompt: A team deletes the gender column from its table "so that the model cannot discriminate". What is the consequence?
options: The model's errors are now equal for women and men
Nothing changes, because gender was not predictive
The model becomes less accurate for everyone
Errors can still differ by gender, and the team can no longer measure whether they do
questions.explanation: Other features and the make-up of the data can carry differences between groups. The attribute is kept outside the model, with a stated purpose, so that errors can be audited.
misconceptions: Believes that an unused column guarantees equal errors
Assumes the column mattered only as a feature, not for the audit
Predicts a general loss of accuracy from removing one column

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most useful limit in a model card?
options: "At sites that opened after training, probabilities ran four points low: use the rank there, not the number."
"The model may not generalise to all settings."
"The model was trained with gradient-boosted trees."
"The model reaches an average precision of 0.55."
questions.explanation: A useful limit names a situation the reader can recognise and says what to do in it, with the measurement behind it.
misconceptions: Is true of every model and tells the reader nothing to act on
States a method, not a limit
States a result, not where it stops holding

questions.prompt: A model ranks benefit applicants by the risk of an incomplete file, so that case workers can call them first. Which statement belongs in the card under "the human decision"?
options: "Applicants above 0.7 are rejected automatically."
"The model is 91% accurate."
"The score orders a case worker's call list; it never decides eligibility, and a case worker may call anyone."
"Case workers must follow the ranking."
questions.explanation: The statement says who decides and what the score may never decide. It keeps a ranking for support from turning into a decision about a person.
misconceptions: Turns a support ranking into an automatic decision about a person
Gives a number where a responsibility is asked for
Removes the judgment of the person who is accountable
